one_liner: Header-only C++17 vector template that unrolls element-wise operators at compile time for compiler auto-vectorization; beat a scalar shader loop 9.4x.
what_it_does: pure_simd::vector<T, N, Align = 32> is an aligned, std::array-like struct whose arithmetic, bitwise, comparison, min/max, abs/round, cast, permute and select operations apply element-wise. load_from, store_to, scalar and iota build and spill vectors; unroll_loop splits a loop of any length into power-of-two step bodies so tails are handled; transform, accumulate, inner_product and sum mirror the standard algorithms with a VectorSize template parameter. It is not a drop-in replacement: you rewrite a scalar loop body in terms of vector types, as the repo's shader example does.
how_it_is_fast: There are no intrinsics: each operator expands into N independent scalar operations through index_sequence pack expansion, and the compiler's SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorizer is expected to fuse them into SIMD instructions. Even without fusion, the expansion interleaves N independent dependency chains, which is effectively manual outer-loop vectorization of the pixel loop; clang does not do this for the plain scalar loop, whose 99-step serial chain per pixel leaves it latency-bound. The maintainer later wrote in issue #6 (2020-05-23) that clang's IR for the new shader example was not vectorized at all and that he 'didn't expect simple code expansion to make such a big difference', so part or all of the gain may be instruction-level parallelism rather than SIMD.
when_to_use: Loops whose iterations are independent but whose body is a long serial dependency chain (per-pixel shaders, per-element iterative integer or float math), where the compiler will not vectorize the outer loop by itself.
Element-wise transforms over int, float or double arrays built with clang or gcc at -O3 -march=native, when you want portable source with no intrinsics and are willing to read the generated assembly.
Small projects that can vendor one 643-line BSD-3-Clause header and need nothing beyond C++17.
Tuning vector width as an unroll knob: widths 8 to 64 helped in the README shader (28.0 ms down to 10.9 ms) while 128 hurt.
when_not_to_use: Reductions and horizontal tests (sum, all-ones or all-zeros checks): in issue #9 gcc 10 did not vectorize them and clang's output loaded data with scalar 4-byte moves; the maintainer recommended intrinsics for that pattern.
Small element types such as uint8 byte streams: the maintainer reported only slight gains over 128-bit intrinsics on an ASCII validation test (issue #6).

When you need predictable codegen or rich SIMD features (masks, shuffles, gathers, vector math functions): results depend on the compiler and the chosen width (the maintainer found clang 9 sensitive to vector size and gcc 7.5 not), so an intrinsics-backed library is safer.
MSVC or any compiler without strong SLP vectorization; the README lists 'C++17 & SLP vectorization' as the requirement and names only gcc and clang.
Production code that needs a stable API: the README calls the library experimental with drastically changing interfaces, and there have been no commits since 2021-10-04.

integration.dependencies: none for include/pure_simd.hpp; Conan with Google Benchmark 1.5.0 and GoogleTest 1.10.0 for the tests and benchmarks
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 with an SLP-vectorizing compiler (gcc or clang); published numbers used clang++ 9.0 with -O3 -march=native
integration.platforms: any target in principle (standard C++, no intrinsics; native_vectorsize reads __AVX512*__/__AVX__ to guess register width), but example/shader.cpp, and so the benchmark and test binaries, includes <x86intrin.h> and builds only on x86
integration.thread_safety: not documented; vectors are plain value types and the header has no global state

gotchas: The README attributes the shader speedup to SIMD, but after the 2020-05-17 rewrite that produced the README table the maintainer reported (issue #6, 2020-05-23) that clang did not vectorize the new shader example at all. The README's width-64 time is about 0.42 ns per pixel-iteration against 3.97 ns scalar (derived from page data: 512 x 512 x 99 iterations), and no IR or assembly is published, so it is unclear which build the table came from; check your own compiler's output before relying on it.

Harness defect in the second example: example/sum.hpp pure_simd_add_bits uses VECTOR_SIZE 16, but scatter_bits of one uint8_t fills only lanes 0-7 while the loop advances one source byte per 16 targets, so it reads half the bit stream, never updates lanes 8-15 and computes a different result from scalar_add_bits; its unit test (n = 8) loads and stores 16 ints from an 8-int array, an out-of-bounds access that passes by accident. For int targets the sum benchmark's factors (1/100, 1/10000, 1/1000000) also cast to 0. The sum benchmark has no published numbers, so the catalogued shader claim is unaffected.

The shader workload relies on signed 32-bit overflow (px*py terms exceed INT_MAX), which is undefined behaviour in both the scalar and the vector version; the repo's equality test passing shows only that the author's build happened to agree. The example also indexes rows by SCRHEIGHT instead of SCRWIDTH, harmless only because the buffer is square.

The header includes only <climits>, <functional> and <cmath> yet uses std::max on an initializer list, std::clamp, std::transform, std::array, std::index_sequence and std::reverse_iterator, so it depends on transitive includes; include <algorithm>, <array>, <utility> and <iterator> first. accumulate and inner_product return a per-lane vector, not a scalar (reduce with sum), and gather_bits was broken on clang until the final commit (issue #9, fixed 2021-10-04).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over EVE or the Vector Class Library only when you want a tiny intrinsic-free header that coaxes gcc or clang into vectorizing or interleaving an existing scalar loop and you will inspect the assembly; for guaranteed SIMD codegen, reductions, byte-level work or vector math functions EVE and VCL are safer, and ISPC is the mature tool for the same one-lane-per-pixel shader pattern.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Core i7-9750H under Ubuntu 18.04 with clang++ 9.0 -O3 -march=native (Google Benchmark 1.5.0, mean of 10 repetitions via scripts/benchmark.sh), a 512x512 integer shader with a 99-step serial chain per pixel took 103 ms as the author's plain scalar loop and 10.9 ms with pure_simd width 64 (about 9.4x, derived from page data); width 8 took 28.0 ms and width 128 regressed to 158 ms. The baseline is the author's own latency-bound scalar loop that the compiler did not vectorize, not a standard-library routine or another SIMD library, and the test checks every width's output against it.
status_note: Abandoned since 2021-10-04 (41 commits, all three issues closed, README says experimental), but BSD-3-Clause and a single 643-line header, so it is easy to vendor as a pattern; its benefit depends on the compiler, so verify codegen on yours.
